danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Næppe havde Pierre lagt hovedet på puden, før han følte sig synke i søvn, men pludselig, næsten med virkelighedens klarhed, hørte han bum, bum, bum af skydning, drønet af projektiler, stønnen og skrig, og han lugtede blod og krudt, og en følelse af rædsel og dødsangst greb ham. Fuld af frygt slog han øjnene op og løftede hovedet fra under sin kappe. Alt var roligt i gården. Kun en ordonnans gik gennem porten og plaskede i mudderet og talte med kroværten. Over Pierres hoved flagrede nogle duer, forstyrret af den bevægelse, han havde gjort, da han satte sig op, under det mørke tag. Hele gårdspladsen var gennemtrængt af en stærk, fredelig lugt af stald, der i dette øjeblik var vidunderlig for Pierre. Han kunne se den klare stjernehimmel mellem de mørke tage.

»Gud ske lov, det er forbi!« tænkte han og trak kappen over hovedet igen. »Å, hvor frygt er en forfærdelig ting, og hvor skammeligt at give efter for den! Men de... de var hele tiden rolige og fattet, lige til det sidste...« tænkte han.

De betød i Pierres sind soldaterne, dem der havde været ved batteriet, dem der havde givet ham mad, og dem der havde bedt foran ikonet. De, disse fremmede mennesker, han ikke tidligere havde kendt, stod klart og skarpt ud fra alle andre.

»At være soldat, bare en simpel soldat!« tænkte Pierre, mens han faldt i søvn, »at træde helt ind i fællesskabets liv, at gennemsyres af det, der gør dem til dem, de er. Men hvordan kaster man alt det overflødige, djævelske af sin ydre person? Der var en tid, hvor jeg kunne have gjort det. Jeg kunne have løbet hjemmefra, som jeg ville. Eller jeg kunne være blevet sendt ud som soldat efter duellen med Dolkhov (Hélènes tidligere elsker).« Og erindringen om middagen i Den Engelske Klub, hvor han havde udfordret Dolokhov, blitzede gennem Pierres sind, og så huskede han sin velgører i Torssjok. Og nu viste billedet af et højtideligt logemøde sig for hans indre blik. Det fandt sted i Den Engelske Klub, og nogen nær og kær sad for enden af bordet. »Ja, det er ham! Det er min velgører. Men han er død!« tænkte Pierre. »Ja, han døde, og jeg vidste ikke, at han var i live. Hvor er jeg ked af, at han er død, og hvor er jeg glad for, at han lever igen!« På den ene side af bordet sad Anatole, Dolokhov, Nesvitskij, Denisov og andre af den slags (i hans drøm var den kategori, disse mænd tilhørte, lige så klart defineret i hans sind som kategorien af dem, han kaldte de), og han hørte disse folk, Anatole og Dolokhov, råbe og synge højt; og dog hørtes hans velgørers stemme hele tiden igennem deres råben, og lyden af hans ord var lige så vægtig og uafbrudt som bulderet på slagmarken, men behagelig og trøstende. Pierre forstod ikke, hvad hans velgører sagde, men han vidste (tankekategorierne var også ganske tydelige i hans drøm), at han talte om godheden og muligheden for at være det, de var. Og de omgav med deres enkle, venlige, faste ansigter hans velgører på alle sider. Men skønt de var venlige, så de ikke på Pierre og kendte ham ikke. Da han ønskede at tale og tiltrække deres opmærksomhed, rejste han sig, men i det øjeblik blev hans ben kolde og bare.

Han skammede sig og dækkede med den ene arm sine ben, som kappen ganske rigtigt var gledet af. Et øjeblik, mens han rettede på kappen, åbnede Pierre øjnene og så de samme halvtage, stolper og gårdspladsen, men nu var alt blåligt, oplyst og glimtende af rim eller dug.

»Det er daggry,« tænkte Pierre. »Men det er ikke det, jeg vil. Jeg vil høre og forstå min velgørers ord.« Igen dækkede han sig til med kappen, men nu var hverken logen eller hans velgører der. Der var kun tanker, klart udtrykt i ord, tanker som nogen udtalte, eller som han selv formulerede.

Bagefter, da han genkaldte disse tanker, var Pierre overbevist om, at nogen uden for ham selv havde udtalt dem, skønt dagens indtryk havde fremkaldt dem. Det forekom ham, at han aldrig var i stand til at tænke og udtrykke sine tanker på den måde, når han var vågen.

»At udholde krig er den vanskeligste underkastelse af menneskets frihed under Guds lov,« havde stemmen sagt. »Enkelhed er underkastelse under Guds vilje; du kan ikke undslippe Ham. Og de er enkle. De taler ikke, men handler. Det talte ord er sølv, men det utalte er guld. Mennesket kan ikke være herre over noget, så længe det frygter døden, men den, der ikke frygter den, ejer alt. Hvis der ingen lidelse fandtes, ville mennesket ikke kende sine grænser, ikke kende sig selv. Det sværeste« (Pierre fortsatte med at tænke, eller høre, i sin drøm) »er at kunne forene meningen med alt i sin sjæl. At forene alt?« spurgte han sig selv. »Nej, ikke at forene. Tanker kan ikke forenes, men at spænde alle disse tanker sammen er, hvad vi har brug for! Ja, man må spænde dem for, spænde dem for!« gentog han for sig selv med indre henrykkelse, idet han følte, at disse ord og de alene udtrykte, hvad han ville sige, og løste det spørgsmål, der plagede ham.
»Ja, man skal spænde for, det er tid at spænde for.«
»Det er tid at spænde for, tid at spænde for, Deres Excellence! Deres Excellence!« gentog en stemme. »Vi må spænde for, det er tid at spænde for...«

Det var staldkarlens stemme, der prøvede at vække ham. Solen skinnede lige ind i Pierres ansigt. Han kiggede ud over den beskidte krogård, i hvis midte soldater vandede deres magre heste ved pumpen, mens vogne kørte ud af porten. Pierre vendte sig bort med afsky og lukkede øjnene og faldt hurtigt tilbage på vognsædet. »Nej, det vil jeg ikke, jeg vil ikke se og forstå dét. Jeg vil forstå, hvad der åbenbarede sig for mig i min drøm. Et sekund mere, og jeg ville have forstået det hele! Men hvad skal jeg gøre? Spænde for, men hvordan kan jeg spænde alting for?« Og Pierre følte med rædsel, at meningen med alt, hvad han havde set og tænkt i drømmen, var gået tabt.
Staldkarlen, kusken og kroværten fortalte Pierre, at en officer var kommet med nyheden om, at franskmændene allerede var tæt på Mosjajsk, og at deres egne tropper var på vej bort.
Pierre rejste sig og bad dem spænde for og indhente ham, hvorefter han gik til fods gennem byen.

Tropperne var på march og efterlod omkring ti tusinde sårede. Der lå sårede i gårdene, i husenes vinduer, og gaderne var fulde af dem. I gaderne, omkring de vogne, der skulle fragte nogle af de sårede bort, hørtes råb, forbandelser og slag. Pierre tilbød sin vogn, der havde indhentet ham, til en såret general, han kendte, og kørte med ham til Moskva. På vejen fik Pierre at vide om svogeren Anatoles død og om fyrst Andrej Bolkonskijs (hans gamle ven) død.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Pierre had barely laid his head on the pillow before he felt himself falling asleep, but suddenly — with almost the vividness of reality — he heard the boom, boom, boom of firing, the thud of projectiles, groans and cries, and smelled blood and powder, and a feeling of horror and dread of death seized him. He opened his eyes in fright and lifted his head from under his cloak. Everything in the yard was peaceful. Only someone's orderly splashed through the mud at the gate, chatting with the innkeeper. Above Pierre's head, some pigeons — disturbed by his movement — fluttered under the dark roof of the shed. The whole courtyard was filled with a strong, peaceful smell of stables, which Pierre found delightful at that moment. He could see the clear, starry sky between the dark roofs of two sheds.

"Thank God — no more of that!" he thought, pulling the cloak back over his head. "Oh, what a terrible thing fear is, and how shamefully I gave in to it! But they... they were steady and calm to the very end..." he thought.

They, in Pierre's mind, were the soldiers — those at the battery, those who had given him food, those who had prayed before the icon. They — those strange men he hadn't known before — stood out sharply and clearly from everyone else.

"To be a soldier, just a common soldier!" Pierre thought as he fell asleep. "To merge completely into that communal life, to be filled with whatever makes them who they are. But how do you shed all the superfluous, devilish burden of the outer man? There was a time I could have done it. I could have run away from my father, as I wanted to. Or I might have been sent into the army after the duel with Dolokhov." And the memory of the dinner at the English Club, when he had challenged Dolokhov, flashed through his mind, and then he remembered his benefactor at Torzhok. And now he pictured a solemn Masonic meeting at the English Club, and someone dear and familiar sat at the end of the table. "Yes, that's him! My benefactor. But he died!" thought Pierre. "Yes, he died, and I didn't know he was alive. How sorry I am that he died, and how glad I am that he's alive again!" On one side of the table sat Anatole, Dolokhov, Nesvitsky, Denisov, and others like them (in his dream this category was as clearly defined as the category he called they), and he heard those people — Anatole and Dolokhov — shouting and singing loudly; yet through their noise, the voice of his benefactor could be heard speaking continuously, and the sound of his words was as weighty and unbroken as the booming on the battlefield, but pleasant and comforting. Pierre couldn't make out what his benefactor was saying, but knew (the categories of thought were perfectly distinct in the dream) that he was speaking of goodness and the possibility of being what they were. And they, with their simple, kind, firm faces, surrounded his benefactor on all sides. But though they were kindly, they didn't look at Pierre and didn't know him. Wanting to speak and draw their attention, he started to rise, but at that moment his legs grew cold and bare.

He felt embarrassed, and with one arm covered his legs from which his cloak had in fact slipped. For a moment, as he adjusted it, Pierre opened his eyes and saw the same shed roofs, posts, and yard, but now everything was tinged with blue, sparkling with frost or dew.

"It's dawn," Pierre thought. "But that's not what I want. I want to hear and understand my benefactor's words." He pulled the cloak over himself again, but now neither the lodge nor his benefactor was there. Only thoughts remained — thoughts clearly expressed in words, thoughts that someone was saying or that he himself was forming.

Afterward, when he recalled those thoughts, Pierre was convinced they had been spoken by someone outside himself, though the impressions of that day had prompted them. He had never, it seemed to him, been able to think and express his thoughts so clearly when awake.

"To endure war is the most difficult submission of human freedom to the law of God," the voice had said. "Simplicity is submission to the will of God; you cannot escape Him. And they are simple. They don't talk — they act. The spoken word is silver, but the unspoken word is golden. Man can master nothing while he fears death, but he who does not fear it possesses everything. If there were no suffering, man would not know his limits — would not know himself. The hardest thing" — Pierre went on thinking, or hearing, in his dream — "is to unite in your soul the meaning of everything. To unite everything?" he asked himself. "No, not unite. You can't unite thoughts. But to harness all these thoughts together — that is what we need! Yes, harness them — harness them!" he repeated to himself with inner ecstasy, feeling that these words alone expressed what he wanted to say and solved the question that tormented him.
"Yes, one must harness — it is time to harness."
"Time to harness, time to harness, your excellency! Your excellency!" a voice kept repeating. "We must harness — it is time to harness..."

It was the voice of the groom, trying to wake him. The sun shone straight into Pierre's face. He glanced at the dirty inn yard where soldiers were watering their thin horses at the pump while carts passed out through the gate. Pierre turned away with distaste and, closing his eyes, quickly fell back onto the carriage seat. "No, I don't want that — I don't want to see and understand that. I want to understand what was being revealed to me in my dream. One more second and I would have grasped it all! But what should I do? Harness — but how can I harness everything?" And Pierre felt with horror that the meaning of everything he had seen and thought in the dream was crumbling away.
The groom, the coachman, and the innkeeper told Pierre that an officer had come with news that the French were already near Mozhaysk and that the Russian forces were leaving the town.
Pierre got up and, telling them to harness the horses and overtake him, set off on foot through the town.

The troops were moving out, leaving about ten thousand wounded behind. Wounded men were visible in the yards, at the windows of houses, and the streets were packed with them. In the streets, around the carts that were to carry some of the wounded away, shouts, curses, and blows could be heard. Pierre offered his carriage, which had caught up with him, to a wounded general he knew, and drove with him to Moscow. On the way, Pierre learned of the deaths of his brother-in-law Anatole and of Prince Andrew.
